The free plan covers search; the full systematic review workflow needs Pro or higher.

threads_text: Elicit searches about 138 million papers and can screen and pull data from them for a literature review. Librarians still say use it to start, not as your only search. Would you trust an AI to screen papers for your thesis?

slides.headline: How to use *Elicit* for a literature review

slides.heading: 1. Ask a *focused question*
paras: Two or three sentences at most. Put your inclusion rules or PICO in Additional Context.
Pick Keyword search for a formal review, Semantic search to explore.

slides.heading: 2. Let it *screen* the papers
paras: Elicit writes screening criteria from your question. Edit them, then run screening.
Every excluded paper shows which rule it failed, and you can overrule it.

slides.heading: 3. Pull the data into a *table*
paras: Name each column in plain English, test a few first, then run extraction.
Click any cell to see the quote it came from.

slides.heading: 4. Check it, then *export*
paras: A 2026 study found Elicit can help human data extractors, not replace them.
Export tables as CSV, sources as RIS or BIB for Zotero.

slides.hook: Follow for guides that save you hours on research, homework and work.

site_article.headline: How to use Elicit for a literature review, step by step
site_article.dek: Elicit searches about 138 million papers and can screen them and pull data into a table. Here is how each step works, which plan you need and where it falls short.
site_article.summary: Elicit is an AI research assistant that searches about 138 million academic papers from Semantic Scholar, PubMed and OpenAlex. Its Systematic Review workflow gathers papers, screens them against criteria, extracts data into a table and writes a report, and it needs the Pro plan or higher.

site_article.seo_description: How to use Elicit for a literature review: ask a focused question, search 138M papers, screen abstracts, extract data, export to Zotero, and the plan you need.
site_article.answer_summary: Start a Systematic Review in Elicit with a short, focused question, let it gather papers, edit and run its screening criteria, then extract data into columns and check the quotes behind each cell. For a quick overview, use a Research Report or the Research Agent instead, which also work on the free plan with limited usage.

paragraphs.text: Elicit is an AI research assistant built for academic literature. If you want to know how to use Elicit for a literature review, the short answer is this: ask a focused question, let Elicit gather papers from its index of about 138 million, screen them against criteria you can edit, and pull the results into a table where every cell links back to a quote. The full Systematic Review workflow needs a paid plan; searching is free.

According to Elicit's help center, its papers come from Semantic Scholar, PubMed and OpenAlex, updated weekly. It includes preprints from arXiv, bioRxiv, medRxiv and SSRN, plus open access and subscription papers, but not books or dissertations. You can also search ClinicalTrials.gov by picking the clinical trials corpus. Elicit reads the full text of open access papers; for paywalled papers it only sees the title and abstract unless you upload the PDF or use its browser extension with your own subscription.
Pick the right tool in Elicit

Elicit now has three main ways to work. The Research Agent answers a question in plain language and can reach beyond papers, to the web, trial registries and files you upload. A Research Report searches, screens and extracts automatically and writes a structured answer, with templates such as General Review, 1-Page Overview and Research Gap Analysis. The Systematic Review is the step by step workflow where you control every stage. The older Find Papers, Extract Data and Chat with Papers tools were replaced by the Research Agent.

Use a Research Report when you need a fast map of a topic or a list of seed papers. Use the Systematic Review when you need to show your method, such as screening criteria and reasons for each exclusion, to a supervisor or a journal.
How to run a literature review in Elicit

paragraphs.title: 1. Write a short, focused question
paragraphs.text: On the setup page, Elicit asks for your research question. Its help center recommends two or three sentences at most. Put the details, such as population, intervention, comparison and outcome, or your inclusion rules, in the Additional Context box instead of the question itself.

paragraphs.title: Question template to copy
paragraphs.text:
Research question: Does [intervention] improve [outcome] in [population] compared with [comparison]?

Additional context: Include randomized controlled trials and cohort studies published since [year]. Exclude studies in [group you want to leave out]. I care most about [main outcome] and [secondary outcome].

paragraphs.title: 2. Choose the stages and the search type
paragraphs.text: Gather, Extraction and Report are always on. Abstract screening and Full-text screening can be switched off; turning off abstract screening also turns off full-text screening. Then pick Keyword search, which supports AND, OR and NOT and suits formal reviews, or Semantic search, which is better for exploring a topic.

paragraphs.title: 3. Gather papers
paragraphs.text: The first search pulls in up to 1,000 papers. You can add more searches in new tabs, upload your own PDFs or bring in papers from your Elicit Library. A review holds up to 5,000 papers on Pro, 20,000 on Scale and 40,000 on Enterprise. When the list looks right, click Define screening.

paragraphs.title: 4. Screen abstracts, then full texts
paragraphs.text: Elicit writes screening criteria from your question. You can edit, switch off or add criteria before you click Run screening. Each excluded paper shows the criterion it failed and why, and you can mark any paper Include or Exclude yourself. For full-text screening, papers that only have an abstract need a PDF upload or the browser extension.

paragraphs.title: 5. Extract data into columns
paragraphs.text: Add columns for what you want from each paper, such as sample size, study design or main result. The help center suggests plain English column names and testing a few columns on a small set first. Then click Run extraction. Click any cell to see the quote from the paper that supports it.

paragraphs.title: Column ideas to copy
paragraphs.text:
Sample size (number of participants analyzed)
Study design (RCT, cohort, case control, other)
Population (age, country, setting)
Main outcome and how it was measured
Main result (effect size with confidence interval if reported)
Limitations the authors mention

paragraphs.title: 6. Generate the report and export
paragraphs.text: The Report step writes up the highest scoring papers: 80 by default, up to 135 on Pro and up to 200 on Scale and Enterprise. Reports download as PDF or Word. Tables export as CSV or Excel, and source lists export as RIS or BIB, which you can import into Zotero, Mendeley or EndNote to format citations in any style.
Which Elicit plan you need

The free Basic plan includes unlimited search across the 138 million papers, unlimited summaries and chat, and limited use of the Research Agent and Research Reports, according to Elicit's pricing page. Plus adds table exports and more extraction columns. The Systematic Review workflow starts at Pro, which Elicit lists at $49 a month on monthly billing, with lower prices on yearly billing. Scale adds live collaboration and extraction from figures, and dual human review is only on Enterprise.
Where Elicit falls short

Elicit's own help center says gray literature and some trial reports are harder to find, and that some regional publications, including some Chinese journals, are missing, so it suggests adding specialized databases. A University of British Columbia library wiki cites a 2026 study in Research Synthesis Methods that found Elicit's data extraction can complement human extractors but not replace them, and the librarians recommend it for early stage searching and finding seed papers rather than as the only search for a systematic review.

In practice, the time saving is real for the first pass: finding papers you missed, drafting criteria and filling a first version of a data table. The risk is trusting a cell without opening its quote. Check every extracted number you plan to report, keep your own record of why papers were excluded, and run the same search in at least one database your field expects, such as PubMed or Scopus.

Before you run extraction on hundreds of papers, run it on ten you already know well. If Elicit gets those wrong, rename the column more precisely and try again. It uses less of your monthly allowance than fixing a full table later.
